messages.subject: Re: GAM
messages.body_plain:
Hi S group members :)

Sorry for this long-winded e-mail on an issu that may seem elementary.
I have doubts in the ways of obtaining components of the Iterative
reweighted least square for gam(). I have tried looking into the book by
McCullagh and Nelder(Generalized linear model), and that by Hastie and
Tibshirani (Generalized additive model), but there were no computational
details that I could find on this particular aspect (Perhaps I overlooked
them).

My problem is in calculating "partial differential of
the
link function with respect to the logit", ie., in the setting of an
iretative reweighted least square setting, the differential that forms
an
inner product with the response residual in the construction of
anadjusted
dependent variable (See TJ Hastie, RJ Tibshirani. Generalized additive
models. Page 141. Algorithm 6.1 Step (ii)). To be explicit, I am
referring to 

z[i] = nu[i]{0} + (y[i] - mu[i]{0}) * (partial differentiate nu[i] with
respect to mu[i])[0]

where nu{0}=alpha[0] + sigma[j=1 to p]f[j]{0}(x[ij]) and
nu[i]{0}=g(mu[i]{0}).

Weights as below need to be constructed, where:

w[i] = partial differentiate mu[i] with respect to nu[i])[0]{2}*(Inverse
of
V[i]{0})

Allow me to use [] to refer to ubscript, and {} to refer to superscript.

I have the following understanding, and please rectify me if I got it
wrong:

(1) The term (partial differentiate nu[i] with respect to mu[i])[0]

can be estimated by the following S-plus command:

term1<-resid(gam(),type=response)/resid(gam(),type=working)

(2) The elements of V[i]{0} can be calculated by the following S-plus
command:

term2<-resid(gam(),type=response)/(resid(gam(),type=pearson)^2)

If I were correct thus far, then, in the spirit of (1) and (2)
production,
I can calculate the final weights, w[i] using the notation above, by the
following S-plus command:

weights<-(ginverse(diag(term2)))(term1^-2)

Sorry for the long-windedness of this e-mail. I hope I have made myself
clear.

Thank you.

Dr. Hin

messages.subject: Several ifelse in one pass?
messages.body_plain:
Hello S-users,

S+6 on Windows NT,
is it possible to reduce the following calls to ifelse to one pass, i.e.
checking the value of "formule" only once?  Of course without doing a for
loop unless someone tells me a for loop is the best solution in such a
case.  The data set is big, very big, close to 2 million records.  What I
want to do is simple: modify the value of three variables based on the
value of a factor variable.

ttt.enc <- ifelse(inc.all[, 'formule'] == '2', inc.all[, 'encincf'] * 1.1,
              ifelse(inc.all[, 'formule'] == '5', inc.all[, 'encincf'] * 0.90,
                      inc.all[, 'encincf']))

ttt.enc15 <- ifelse(inc.all[, 'formule'] == '2', inc.all[, 'en15inci'] * 1.1,
              ifelse(inc.all[, 'formule'] == '5', inc.all[, 'en15inci'] * 0.90,
                      inc.all[, 'en15inci']))

ttt.uni <- ifelse(inc.all[, 'formule'] == '2', inc.all[, 'unsousi'] * 1.1,
                ifelse(inc.all[, 'formule'] == '5', inc.all[, 'unsousi'] * 0.90,
                      inc.all[, 'unsousi']))

I also thought of using apply as following:

ttt.out <- t(apply(inc.all[, c('formule', 'encincf', 'en15incf', 'unsousi')], 1,
                 FUN = function(y){
                   y <- as.numeric(y)
                   if (y[1] == 2) y[2:4] * 1.1
                   else if (y[1] == 5) y[2:4] * 0.9
                   else y[2:4]
                 }))

It seems to work, it is still running, but what bothers me in this approach is 
the fact that "formule" is a factor and the other variables
are numeric, therefore when a row is passed to FUN all variables are converted 
to character;  the conversion back to numeric works
in this case since the levels of "formule" are valid numerical values, but it 
wouldn't work for a general factor variable.  Furthermore in
the conversion to character and then back to numeric we are probably loosing 
some numerical accuracies?  Would a for loop be the
best way of doing what I want to do or is there better ways?

Thanks to all,

Gérald Jean

messages.subject: quirks of importdata (win)
messages.body_plain:
S-PLUS 2000, Win98. This took me some hours to figure out. Thought I'd 
share it.

1. The importData() function won't totally overwrite existing data in the 
dataframe you specify. Let's say you have a three-column dataframe called 
"temp" with columns a,b,c and want to import a new dataframe with columns 
d,e. Then if you specify just importData(DataFrame="temp",...) columns a,b 
will be replaced with d,e but column c will be kept. Make sure you replace 
the old dataframe with temp <- null().

2. You have to use guiEval() to make sure that importData works all right. 
I kept getting curious errors where some column names would be replaced 
with "V1" "V2" and so forth at random, even after I fixed problem (1).

Are these bugs or features ? Are these behaviours present in the new 
version of S-PLUS ?

This is the function that occasioned the problem (after they're fixed). I'm 
trying to read in datasets for a set of symptoms and append them.

readsympts <- function(sympts,datadir,filesuffix)
{       
        result <- null()
        for (ii in sympts) {
                file <- paste(datadir,ii,filesuffix,sep="")
                tempf <- null()
                guiEval(tempf <- import.data(DataFrame = "tempf",
                FileName = file,FileType="ASCII"),obj.name="tempf")

                guiClose("DataFrame","tempf")
                result <- rbind(result,data.frame(tempf,outc=ii))               
        }
        return(result)
}

Yours,
Jan Brogger,
University of Bergen, Norway

messages.subject_clean: Questions on Correlations for hierarchical data and combining bootstrap() and MI from Hmisc.
messages.body_plain:
Dear Splus people,

I have a two-part question: firstly to find out what kind of approaches I 
could use to analyze a dataset with a certain hypothesis in mind, and 
secondly to try to find out why what I'm trying doesn't seem to work.

The problem: two characteristics of interest have been measured on eight 
genera of different leaves at two very widely spaced and distinct time 
points.  There are missing data in each characteristic, and I am willing to 
assume that they are missing completely at random.  I have quite different 
sample sizes for each Period.Genus combination, ranging from 1 (!) to 80.

The question is: have the relative levels of the different genera changed 
in time for either characteristic?

My tentative solution is to perform on the means either a Friedman test or 
a correlation test (so the Genus mean is treated as the observation and I'm 
comparing them across periods), whilst taking account of the missing 
data.  I can do this with multiple imputation from the Hmisc library; it 
works with no problem.  But in any case I can't see an obvious to account 
for the fact that the means are estimated from samples.

So I tried to develop some bootstrap-like idea, where I would resample 
within the groups, multiply impute, fit the model, extract the 
coefficients, estimate the group means, and then calculate the 
correlation.  Repeat about 1000 times.

So, if anyone can suggest any other way that I might incorporate that extra 
uncertainty into my inference, I'd be grateful.  That's the first part.

The following is related to my solution, and it involves the bootstrap and 
imputation from Hmisc.  Since the imputation routine runs fine outside 
bootstrap(), I wasn't sure if this query should go to Professor Harrell or 
to the group.  Clearly, I opted for the latter - I apologize if this was an 
error.

My function won't loop within bootstrap, as it insists that there are 
missing values.  I've converted it so that the bootstrap should never see 
the missing values - it should see them as -999, which are converted to 
missing before imputation.  But somehow they slip by!  I've included the 
code below.

# "Combined" is the initial dataframe, with four variables and numerous MCAR
# observations.  To start: set missing observations to -999.

Combined$C2[is.na(Combined$C2)] <- -999
Combined$C1[is.na(Combined$C1)] <- -999

# Nothing is missing now.  This next function replaces the -999 with 
missing values,

# performs multiple imputation, returns the correlation of the group means 
across Period,

# and converts the NA back to -999 for the bootstrap.  Thus (in theory) the 
dataframe

# should leave unchanged from the way that it entered.

calc.corr <- function(dframe) {

        is.na(dframe$C1[dframe$C1 < -500]) <- T

        is.na(dframe$C2[dframe$C2 < -500]) <- T

        data.mi <- transcan(~ C1 + C2 + Genus + Period, imputed=T, 
n.impute=10, data=dframe, transformed=T)

        mfit <- fit.mult.impute(C1 ~ Genus+Genus:Period-1, lm, data = 
dframe, xtrans = data.mi)

        is.na(dframe$C1[is.na(dframe$C1)]) <- F

        is.na(dframe$C2[is.na(dframe$C2)]) <- F

        return(cor.test(coef(mfit)[1:8], 
coef(mfit)[1:8]+coef(mfit)[9:16])$p.value)

}

# Call this function within bootstrap()

bootstrap(Combined, calc.corr, B=1000, 
group=as.factor((as.integer(Genus)-1)*2 + as.integer(Period)))

==========================

After seemingly running through the exercise once (doing the imputation and 
presenting the variance inflations), this operation forms the replications 
1 to 100, gets through transcan once (as far as I can tell from the 
output), and then returns:

Problem in (function(object, ...): missing values not allowed: found in C1
Use traceback() to see the call stack

> traceback()

22: eval(action, sys.parent())

21: doErrorAction("Problem in (function(object, ...): missing values not 
allowed: found in C1", 1000)

20: stop(paste("missing values not allowed: found in", 
paste(names(object)[err], collapse = ", ")))

19: (function(object, ...)

18: (function(object, ...)

17: model.frame.default(formula = formula, data = completed.data, 
drop.unused.levels = T)

16: model.frame(formula = formula, data = completed.data, 
drop.unused.levels = T)

15: eval(m, sys.parent())

14: fitter(formula, data = completed.data)

13: fit.mult.impute(C1 ~ Genus + Genus:Period - 1, lm, data = dframe, 
xtrans = data.mi)

12: statistic(data)

11: fit.func(inds.mat[, i], data, statistic, args.stat)

10: FUN(...X.sub.i...., function(inds, data, statistic, args.stat)

9: list(

8: NULL

7: lapply(temp, call.stat, fit.func, data, statistic, args.stat, inds.mat)

6: bootstrap(Combined, calc.corr, B = 1000, group = 
as.factor((as.integer(Genus) - 1) * 2 + as.integer(Period)), assign.frame1 = T)

5: eval(i, local)

4: source(auto.print = auto.print, exprs = substitute(exprs.literal))

3: script.run(exprs.literal = {

2: eval(expression(script.run(exprs.literal = {

1:

Message: Problem in (function(object, ...): missing values not allowed: 
found in C1

So, in a nutshell, I can't see how bootstrap is still seeing missing 
values.  I emphasize that if I run the function outside the bootstrap() 
then it returns the correlation with no hesitation.  Also, outside 
bootstrap(), there's no need for the whole conversion of NA to -999 and 
back again deal, it runs just fine without that.  I'm mystified.

So any help for either or both portions of this question would be 
gratefully accepted!

best wishes

Andrew

messages.body_plain:
To my knowledge the construct is.na(x) <- logical value
does not make sense.

transcan was not written to be used inside a bootstrap loop
but this could be done very slowly.  Typically, multiple
imputations will have a variance that is large enough with
respect to other sources of variation that you might get
away with doing the multiple imputations outside a bootstrap
loop.  fit.mult.impute doesn't know about bootstrapping, but
could probably be tricked into working at some cost in
computation time.

I didn't take time to really understand your problem to
offer better advice.

Frank

On Fri, 2 Nov 2001, Frank E Harrell Jr wrote:

> To my knowledge the construct is.na(x) <- logical value
> does not make sense.

It's standard S4, implemented in S-PLUS 6.  It means for each element of x,
set to missing if the corresponding element of the rhs (after recycling) is
true.  Mostly (but not always)

is.na(x) <- l

is equivalent to

x[l] <- NA,

strings (the class) being one exception.  Green Book pp. 199-200.

messages.subject: Memory not getting freed!
messages.body_plain:
Hello S-users,

S+6 on Windows NT4.0, sp 5

why is it that memory doesn't get freed when doing simple tasks?  I thought
S+6 was going to be better at managing memory?  Here is a simple example.

a few commands, not many, since new session start up.
> memory.size()
[1] 325585572
> names(inc.all)[c(8, 16, 25, 21)] <- c('rfum', 'mtass', 'nbsin3an', 'zone')
> memory.size()
[1] 648399684
> memory.size(max = T)
[1] 648399684

assigning new names to four columns of a large data frame uses over 300M of 
memory and that memory is not even freed when the
task is completed, I don't get this!!  As a result of memory not getting freed 
I have to close S+ every 30 minutes or so and start a new
session so there is enough memory to move on with my analysis.  I have lots of 
memory, 1G of RAM and 1G of swapspace, but
this is not enough it seems.  The same problems occur when, for example, I am 
creating new factor variables or merging levels of
existing factors, I can't get anywhere it seems, I always have to close down S+ 
and start a fresh session.  My data set is roughly
250M in size, hence there is room for 8 copies in 2G of memory but again due to 
inadequate memory management I am always
up against a wall with the same error message "Unable to obtain requested ...."

Am I doing something wrong?  Is my set up inadequate?

Thanks for any insights into this problem,

messages.subject: Re: error function
messages.body_plain:
Hi Alesia:

Let me clarify something here before answering your question. The error
function is denoted as erf(x); the complementary error function is denoted
as erfc(x).  Also, erfc(x) = 1 - erf(x).
The error function is very closely related to the standard normal
distribution function, Phi(x). It can be obtained as follows:
erf(x) = 2 * Phi(x * sqrt(2)) - 1
erfc(x) = 2 * (1 - Phi(x * sqrt(2)))

In Splus/R you can compute these as:

erfx <-  2 * pnorm(x * sqrt(2)) - 1
erfcx <- 2 * (1 - pnorm(x * sqrt(2)))

Hope this helps,
Ravi.

messages.subject: negative binomial GLMs and extractAIC
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm using S+2000r2 on NT4.0 to carry out negative binomial glm's using
the glm.nb function from the MASS library. I have a set of a priori
model structures, and want to calculate the AICs and Akaike weights as
described in Burnham and Anderson (Model Selection and Inference, 1998).
I am confused about the sorts of values extractAIC is returning, and
hope someone can straighten me out.

Brief background, AIC is -2 * Log-likelihood + 2*K, where K is the
number of parameters in the model, in B&A's notation. In S+,
extractAIC.negbin(fit), where fit is from glm.nb uses
-fit$twologlik + k*edf
where k defaults to 2 and edf is the number of parameters.
So far I'm alright. twologlik is 2 * the result of a function called
loglik defined inside glm.nb, which looks at least somewhat like
negative binomial probabilities I've written down before.

The problem is, extractAIC.negbin always seems to return negative
values. The sum of logarithms of probabilities should be negative, but
then the negative sign in extractAIC.negbin should yield a positive
value, shouldn't it?

There's nothing wrong with negative AIC's, but in my naivete I had
calculated them myself without the minus sign, before discovering
extractAIC.negbin, and the results were, well, spectacularly different.

I realise that there is more than one way to write down the probability
for a negative binomial distribution, and it looks like some terms
constant in the parameters have been left out of loglik(). Is this why
the twologlik value is positive, rather than a sum of logged
probabilities?

In an effort to understand I modified glm.nb to use a loglik function
based on versions of the negative binomial common in ecology that I've
used before. It doesn't work (yet) so I hereby appeal to a higher
authority.

Many thanks in advance, and humbly awaiting illumination,
Drew

messages.subject: Re: is.na(x) <- logical value
messages.body_plain:
Rolf,

Perhaps you should think more carefully about the construction

> x[1] <- NA

To me this is the anomolous one as it encourages the view that "NA" is "the"
missing value.  This in turn encourages people into traps like  if(any(x ==
NA)) ... which we know does not work and for good reasons.  The new
construction is consistent with the philosophy that you should use a special
function both to set as well to check for missing values.  "is.na<-" is a
natural candidate for the job.

Personally I don't think the new construction is really all that dangerous,
actually.  To me it seems that unless people understand what is going on
there is not much chance they will even use it at all, let alone
incorrectly.  This is precisely *because* it does look so counter-intuitive
if you don't understand it!  

(I'm not about to suggest banning the old construction just yet, either...)

Bill Venables.

messages.subject: Re: negative binomial GLMs and extractAIC
messages.body_plain:
Log-likelihoods and hence AIC are only defined up to an additive constant.
Technically, this depends on the underlying dominating measure used to
form the densities.

extractAIC is a helper function for stepAIC.  For its stated purpose,
those constants don't matter.  It was not designed for your application.

The term omitted is -log y!  It is easy to include by adding - lgamma(y +
1) to the internal function loglik in glm.nb.

messages.subject: Summary: User-Written Help on Windows
messages.body_plain:
The original query was for a method to implement help files for 
user-written functions on S-Plus 6 on Windows.  I thank those many who 
replied:  Brad Biggerstaff, Rich Calaway, Brian Ripley, Nick Ellis, and 
Charla Lambert of Insighful.

BB and BR reminded me that the online supplement to S-Programming was 
available, and indeed it contains more up-to-date information than the book 
itself.  NE confirmed that the approach given there works:

" The information is all available from the link Brian supplied but I 
thought  I'd just say I've built Splus6 help files without problems. I have 
a .bat file in my documentation area that looks like

@echo off
perl d:\projects\Splus\S2html Utilities *.d
hhc Utilities
del *.html Utilities.hhp Utilities.hhc Utilities.hhk S+chm.css

" All my help files are in nroff format (.d files) created by the uprompt 
function which comes with Brian's utilities. The perl script (S2html) 
converts them to html. Then the Microsoft help compiler (hhc, freely 
available) creates a help file (.chm) which you put in the library 
directory containing the .Data."

The easiest approach was suggested by CL, who wrote:

"To write your own help files in S-PLUS 6 for Windows, use the promptHtml() 
function. This creates a skeleton HTML file that you can fill out and place 
in the __Hhelp directory of your project. When the project is in your 
S-PLUS search path, you should be able to view the help file using either 
the help() or "?" functions. Any links you put in the help file to 
functions in other databases will not work, however.

"To write a help set for an entire library of functions, you'll need an 
HTML Help Compiler (such as Microsoft HTML Help Workshop), which creates a 
compiled HTML file (*.chm) from the HTML for your individual functions."

Charla also promised that the error in the Programmer's Guide (in which 
Chapter 4 refers you to Chapter 4, instead of to Chapter 12) will be corrected.

I can confirm that the HTML method works well, and as a bonus it seems to 
come up faster than the S-Plus native help system.

Thanks again to all.

--
Michael Prager      <Mike.Prager at noaa.gov>
NOAA Center for Coastal Fisheries and Habitat Research
Beaufort, North Carolina  28516  USA

messages.body_plain:
At 01:27 PM 11/5/01 -0500, Rosenfeld, Simon (NCI) wrote:
> Does anybody know if the algorithm of Support Vector Machines has been
> implemented in S-PLUS?
> Simon Rosenfeld
> NIH/NCI

Until recently most of the SVM algorithms required some pretty heavy 
quadratic optimization routines (Lagrangian multipliers with inequalities 
etc) which don't appear to standard in S or R.

But recently some new 'generalized' SVM algorithms have been showing up 
which don't need the heavy optimization and therefore should be easier to 
code in any language that supports general linear algebra routines.

Olvi Mangasarian (http://www.cs.wisc.edu/~olvi/) and his student Glenn Fung 
(http://www.cs.wisc.edu/~gfung/) presented a 'proximal SVM' engine at the 
latest KDD which  could they coded in 6 lines of MATLAB and which they 
claim is competitive in performance with the 'classical' SVM engines. 
ftp://ftp.cs.wisc.edu/pub/dmi/tech-reports/01-02.ps

Here is the Fung/Mangasarian MATLAB code for the Proximal SVM. (Sorry, I 
don't know enough S/R to convert even this snippet):

function [w, gamma] = psvm(A,d,nu)
% PSVM: linear and nonlinear classification
% INPUT: A, d=diag(D), nu. OUTPUT: w, gamma
% [w, gamma] = pvm(A,d,nu);

  [m,n]=size(A);e=ones(m,1);H=[A -e];
  v=(d'*H)'                 %v=H'*D*e;
  r=(speye(n+1)/nu+H'*H)\v  % solve (I/nu+H'*H)r=v
  w=r(1:n);gamma=r(n+1);    % getting w,gamma from r

messages.subject: Type I Error Rate and GAM with Smoothing Spline
messages.subject_clean: Type I Error Rate and GAM with Smoothing Spline
messages.body_plain:
I have been running some simulations in which a linear relationship is
modeled and I have ran the significance test for the smoothing spline
fit of degree 4 as a check for any nonlinear component.  To my surprise
the rejection rate for the test is well above the level I expected when
the alpha is set at 0.05.  The error rate is usually around 0.08.

A simplified version of a function is given below.  The following input
is required.

n is the sample size for each of the replications
effect is the slope and correlation between for the relationship
block is the number of replications to perform

linearity.test.fcn_function(n, effect, block)
{
        answer <- matrix(ncol = 1, nrow = block)
        for(i in 1:block) {
                x <- rnorm(n, 0, 30)
                y <- x * effect + rnorm(n, 0, (var(x) * (1 -
effect^2))^0.5)
                answer[i, 1] <- summary(gam(y ~ s(x, 4)))$anova[[4]][2]
        }
        answer
}

As an example the following two simulations gave error rates of 0.083
and 0.0925 much higher than the expected 0.05.  I even ran this using a
sample size of 10000 and the error rate was still too high.

> a_linearity.test.fcn(2000,.3,2000)
> length(a[a<=0.05])/2000
[1] 0.083
> a_linearity.test.fcn(2000,.6,2000)
> length(a[a<=0.05])/2000
[1] 0.0925
> a_linearity.test.fcn(10000,.6,2000)
> length(a[a<=0.05])/2000
[1] 0.084

Am I using the test incorrectly or is the type 1 error rate for this
test higher than it should be?  Any help on this is appreciated.  The
above was run using S-Plus 2000 Professional Release 3 under Windows
2000 Professional.

James Janisse

messages.subject: Fitted Error Model
messages.body_plain:
Dear S News;

I have a dataset of 10,000 experiments with 2 repeats for each experiment.  
Does anyone have experience using a fitted error model as a special case of 
common error (random error is slightly different based on magnitude; 
heteroscedastic error)?  I have a model where there is a slight relationship 
between magnitude and stdev values so I think fitted error would be 
appropriate.  Another approach may be a small sample approach but either way my 
model chokes when I want to remove outliers using only 2 repeats each for the 
10,000 experiments.  My model works great for 3 repeats per experiment but I am 
looking for a model that can estimate outliers using 2 repeats.

Also, thanks once again to Nick Ellis (to whom I should address my questions 
first if only to save bandwidth) and Matt Kurbat who replied about clustering.  
Matt mentioned a method whereby one would use multidimensional scaling and 
check out the first two dimensions to get an idea about the normalized 
clusters.  Nick suggested I use hierarchical clustering since I know the number 
of clusters I want.  K-means would be another route but probabilistic and 
multivariate models exist that actually determine the number of groups based 
only on group variance and data distribution.

Any advice on the fitted error model would be greatly appreciated;

Phillip Stafford

I have sp2000, release3 and I just discovered a "feature" in import.data
from Excel. Just to give a warning after a few wasted hours. 

Here is the critical part of the code:

import.data(FileName = 
paste(DataSourcePaths[k], "\\", as.name(DataSourceFiles[i]), sep = ""),
FileType = "Excel", ColNames = "", Format = "", TargetStartCol
 = "1", DataFrame = paste("path", k, "frame", i, "page", j, sep = ""),
NameRow = NameRow, StartCol = 
"1", EndCol = "END", StartRow = StartRow, EndRow = "END", Delimiters = ",
\\t", 
SeparateDelimiters = F, PageNumber = as.character(j), RowNameCol = "",
StringsAsFactors = "Never", 
VLabelAsNumber = F, DatesAsDoubles = F, Filter = "", OdbcConnection = "",
OdbcSqlQuery = "")
remove(list = as.character(paste("path", k, "frame", i, "page", j, sep =
"")))           ### To avoid data overlapping (an other bug?)

global arguments were:
j <- 1:18 (for)
NameRow <- "1"
StartRow <- "1"

I'm not an expert in importing Excel-sheets but by a trial and error method
I figured out that the NameRow is the source of the problem. Setting NameRow
= "" (default = 1?) and everything went well. Any comments or knowledge
behind the problem (feature)?

I guess it is wise to try avoid Excel importing. I have had other problems
(crushing with NAs in a source file) as well. Keep it simple if you have to
do it anyway!

Regards and best wishes to everybody - I have got a lot from this group,

Jussi Makinen

messages.body_plain:
Dear Greg,

Thank you so much for your helpful reply. I played with postscript()
again and found that you're right. I thought the ps file was not
created properly when I saw warning messages from Gsview. It turns
out that these messages are just warnings and the ps files is indeed
a multiple-page ps file. Furthermore, the warning messages can be
disabled by checking Options -> DSC warnings -> Off in Gsview (v4.0).
Now I am very happy with sqpe + postscript(), which does the same
job as splus + graphsheet() for me. Thanks again.

Paul.

documented ) and HBA1CV1VALUE, HBA1CV2VALUE, HBA1CV3VALUE are variables on

============

Table displaying the mean, sd etc,  for all the variables (HBA1CV1VALUE,
HBA1CV2VALUE, HBA1CV3VALUE) for Males

Results for female:
===============

Table displaying the mean, sd etc,  for all the variables (HBA1CV1VALUE,
HBA1CV2VALUE, HBA1CV3VALUE) for females

Results for Not documented
===============

Table displaying the mean, sd etc,  for all the variables (HBA1CV1VALUE,
HBA1CV2VALUE, HBA1CV3VALUE) for Not documented

I tried to code as shown below:

arg1 <- argsList[[1]]      # vector of all variables  (HBA1CV1VALUE,
HBA1CV2VALUE, HBA1CV3VALUE)
arg2 <- argsList[[2]]      # Grouping variable (GENDER)

for( i in 1:length(arg1) ) {
    j <- arg1[i]
    newDF <- data.frame( df[,j], df[,arg2])
    names(newDF) <- c("Variable","Group")
    gMean <- round( tapply( na.exclude(as.numeric(unlist(newDF$Variable))),
newDF$Group, mean), 2 )

function(x) length(x)-length(na.exclude(x)) )

    names(newDF) <- c( "Non-Missing Cases", "Mean", "SD", "Lower CI", "Upper

}

messages.subject_clean: Genetic and Evolutionary Computation for Signal Processing and Image Analysis
messages.body_plain:
EURASIP JOURNAL ON APPLIED SIGNAL PROCESSING

Special Issue on:

  Genetic and Evolutionary Computation for
  Signal Processing and Image Analysis

Genetic and evolutionary computation has provided effective tools
(genetic algorithms, genetic programming, evolutionary strategies,
etc.) for the development of software or hardware solutions of
complex problems of high industrial and social relevance. Many
applications, ranging from design of low-level algorithms to design
of specific hardware for signal processing and image analysis have
been shown to benefit from evolutionary techniques.

The aim of this special issue is to bring together contributions
about the latest developments in evolutionary computation for signal
processing and image analysis, along with review papers and tutorials
on some of its aspects. The special issue will offer a broad overview
of the potential and the accomplishments of evolutionary computation
techniques in those fields.

The whole spectrum of signal processing/image analysis applications
will be addressed, from low-level 1-D signal processing to high-level
image or multi-dimensional signal analysis. Therefore, topics of
interest for the issue include (but are not limited to):

 - Reviews and tutorials on any aspects of signal processing and
   image analysis by means of evolutionary computation techniques
 - Applications of evolutionary computation to real-life problems
   involving signal analysis and processing
 - Evolvable image analysis and signal processing hardware
 - Evolutionary pattern recognition
 - Hybrid architectures for machine vision and signal processing
   including evolutionary components
 - Comparisons between different evolutionary techniques and between
   evolutionary and non-evolutionary techniques in image analysis
   and signal processing
 - Time series analysis by means of evolutionary computation techniques.

Authors should follow the EURASIP JASP manuscript format described at
the Journal site http://asp.hindawi.com/. Prospective authors should
submit an electronic copy of their complete manuscript through the
EURASIP JASP web submission system at http://asp.hindawi.com/wss/,

messages.subject: Re: SVM's in S-PLUS
messages.body_plain:
I'm not aware of SVM's for S-Plus, but the e1071 package for R includes
SVM's among other tools; see http://lib.stat.cmu.edu/R/CRAN/ for example,
or your nearest mirror.  The easiest route to gain access to this routine
is of course to install R and then install the package, but since the
source code for the R package is available at the site, it should be
possible to port it to S-Plus.  I would guess (though I have no firsthand
knowledge) that most of the work is accomplished by C routines, which would
need to be changed very little if at all to be called by S-Plus rather than
R.

Documentation in the e1071 package indicates that it may not be optimal for
really large datasets, so you would just have to determine for yourself if
it will work for you.

Jim Garrett
Becton Dickinson Diagnostic Systems

> implemented in S-PLUS?
> Simon Rosenfeld
> NIH/NCI

messages.subject: speed up a slow for() loop
messages.subject_clean: speed up a slow for() loop
messages.body_plain:
I am trying to get estimates for some adaptive sampling survey data.  The
program I've written to do the calculations is pathetically slow, and I'd
like to speed it up a bit.

I am calculating the modified Horvitz-Thompson estimator in chapter 4 of
Thompson & Seber's _Adaptive Sampling_ (1991), and I think my program's
getting bogged down with the part where I need to calculate the product of
a ratio of "N choose R"s (see the formula below).

akk' = 1 - (1 - ak) - (1 - ak') +
     [PROD from h=1 to H of {[(Nh - xhk - xhk') choose nh]/(Nh choose nh)}]

Because the "N choose R"s get quite large in my calculations, I expanded
the math within the "N choose R"s so that I could calculate the product of
a series of fractions less than one.  Thus
{[(Nh - xhk - xhk') choose nh]/(Nh choose nh)}
became
[(Nh - xhk - xhk')/(Nh)] *
     [(Nh - xhk - xhk' - 1)/(N -1)] *
     ... *
     [(Nh - xhk - xhk' - nh + 1)/(N - nh + 1)]

The program I wrote to do this is extremely slow (see the sample section
below).  When I ran just the first three iterations for the index "i" on
this sample program, it took about 5 minutes on my computer.  I am sure
that I have not written this program to do the calculations in the most
efficient way, but I am stuck in my thinking about it and am looking for
insights from s-news listers.

I carried out the calculations by writing one long nasty formula as a
character variable and then evaluating it.  I considered the possibility
that it was this choice that was slowing my program down.  So I tried a
rewrite using the Recall() function to calculate the product of the series,
but this did not improve the speed (same real time elapsed).

If you have any suggestions to offer that might speed up this program, I
would greatly appreciate them.  I did a search on the s-news archive, and I
actually found a posting for someone else doing adaptive sampling
calculations, but I found no responses to that posting.  I am using S-PLUS
6.0 Prof. Rel. 2 on Windows NT on dual Pentium II processors with 256 MB
RAM.

Thanks for your help in advance!

JVA

# sample input data
nh <- c(64, 67, 59, 32, 128, 135, 40)
Nh <- c(9195, 1537, 7924, 4347, 36941, 2695, 16241)
alphak <- abs(rnorm(mean=0.05, sd=0.06, n=27))
ystark <- c(exp(rnorm(mean=1.7, sd=1.1, n=20)), rep(0, 7))
xhk <- matrix(sample(rep(0:7, c(168, 10, 5, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1))), nrow=7,
ncol=27)

# calculate the joint inclusion probability
klist <- lapply(nh, function(x) (1:x)-1)
varcontrib <- matrix(0, nrow=length(alphak), ncol=length(alphak))
for(i in 1:3) {               # use this for trial run
#for(i in seq(alphak)) { # this is the real thing
for(j in i:length(alphak)) {
    if(i==j) alphakkprime <- alphak[i] else {
        fractval <- numeric(length(nh))
        for(m in seq(nh)) fractval[m] <- eval(parse(text=
            paste("((Nh[m] - xhk[m, i] - xhk[m, j] - ", klist[[m]],
          ")/(Nh[m] - ", klist[[m]], "))", sep="", collapse="*")))
        alphakkprime <- alphak[i] + alphak[j] - 1 + prod(fractval)
        }
    varcontrib[i, j] <- ystark[i] * ystark[j] / alphakkprime *
     (alphakkprime/(alphak[i]*alphak[j]) - 1)
    }}

messages.subject: Summary - speed up a slow for() loop
messages.subject_clean: Summary - speed up a slow for() loop
messages.body_plain:
Sam Buttrey just offered a wonderful and elegant solution to my problem,
and it speeds things up dramatically.  Thank you, Sam!

My original posting is pasted below (I've edited it to show the correct
denominators, because, as Sam pointed out to me, I wrote some Nhs as Ns
before).

Sam wrote: you need a product of a bunch of ratios of the form (V/W),
(V-1/W-1), (V-2/W-2), and so on down to (V-k/W-k).  You can do this like
so, with V standing for Nh - xhk - xhk', W standing for Nh, and k standing
for nh + 1.
     num <- V:(V-k)
     denom <- W:(W-k)
     prod(num/denom)

To give this a try, I replaced the innermost for() loop in my sample
program,

        for(m in seq(nh)) fractval[m] <- eval(parse(text=
            paste("((Nh[m] - xhk[m, i] - xhk[m, j] - ", klist[[m]],
          ")/(Nh[m] - ", klist[[m]], "))", sep="", collapse="*")))

with

        for(m in seq(nh)) {
            num <- (Nh[m] - xhk[m, i] - xhk[m, j]):(Nh[m] - xhk[m, i] -
xhk[m, j] - nh[m] + 1)
            denom <- Nh[m]:(Nh[m] - nh[m] + 1)
            fractval[m] <- prod(num/denom)
            }

I was able to run the first three iterations of i in 4 seconds (down from 5
minutes)!!!  And I was able to run all of the iterations in just 13
seconds.

This list is great.
Sam ... I owe you one.

JVA

                                                                                
                                  
                    "Jean V Adams"                                              
                                  
                    <jean_adams at usgs.gov>             To:     
s-news at wubios.wustl.edu                             
                    Sent by:                          cc:                       
                                  
                    s-news-owner at lists.biostat        Subject:     [S] speed up 
a slow for() loop                 
                    .wustl.edu                                                  
                                  
                                                                                
                                  
                                                                                
                                  
                    11/07/01 03:00 PM                                           
                                  
                                                                                
                                  
                                                                                
                                  

I am trying to get estimates for some adaptive sampling survey data.  The
program I've written to do the calculations is pathetically slow, and I'd
like to speed it up a bit.

I am calculating the modified Horvitz-Thompson estimator in chapter 4 of
Thompson & Seber's _Adaptive Sampling_ (1991), and I think my program's
getting bogged down with the part where I need to calculate the product of
a ratio of "N choose R"s (see the formula below).

akk' = 1 - (1 - ak) - (1 - ak') +
     [PROD from h=1 to H of {[(Nh - xhk - xhk') choose nh]/(Nh choose nh)}]

Because the "N choose R"s get quite large in my calculations, I expanded
the math within the "N choose R"s so that I could calculate the product of
a series of fractions less than one.  Thus
{[(Nh - xhk - xhk') choose nh]/(Nh choose nh)}
became
[(Nh - xhk - xhk')/(Nh)] *
     [(Nh - xhk - xhk' - 1)/(N -1)] *
     ... *
     [(Nh - xhk - xhk' - nh + 1)/(N - nh + 1)]

The program I wrote to do this is extremely slow (see the sample section
below).  When I ran just the first three iterations for the index "i" on
this sample program, it took about 5 minutes on my computer.  I am sure
that I have not written this program to do the calculations in the most
efficient way, but I am stuck in my thinking about it and am looking for
insights from s-news listers.

I carried out the calculations by writing one long nasty formula as a
character variable and then evaluating it.  I considered the possibility
that it was this choice that was slowing my program down.  So I tried a
rewrite using the Recall() function to calculate the product of the series,
but this did not improve the speed (same real time elapsed).

If you have any suggestions to offer that might speed up this program, I
would greatly appreciate them.  I did a search on the s-news archive, and I
actually found a posting for someone else doing adaptive sampling
calculations, but I found no responses to that posting.  I am using S-PLUS
6.0 Prof. Rel. 2 on Windows NT on dual Pentium II processors with 256 MB
RAM.

Thanks for your help in advance!

JVA

# sample input data
nh <- c(64, 67, 59, 32, 128, 135, 40)
Nh <- c(9195, 1537, 7924, 4347, 36941, 2695, 16241)
alphak <- abs(rnorm(mean=0.05, sd=0.06, n=27))
ystark <- c(exp(rnorm(mean=1.7, sd=1.1, n=20)), rep(0, 7))
xhk <- matrix(sample(rep(0:7, c(168, 10, 5, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1))), nrow=7,
ncol=27)

# calculate the joint inclusion probability
klist <- lapply(nh, function(x) (1:x)-1)
varcontrib <- matrix(0, nrow=length(alphak), ncol=length(alphak))
for(i in 1:3) {               # use this for trial run
#for(i in seq(alphak)) { # this is the real thing
for(j in i:length(alphak)) {
    if(i==j) alphakkprime <- alphak[i] else {
        fractval <- numeric(length(nh))
        for(m in seq(nh)) fractval[m] <- eval(parse(text=
            paste("((Nh[m] - xhk[m, i] - xhk[m, j] - ", klist[[m]],
          ")/(Nh[m] - ", klist[[m]], "))", sep="", collapse="*")))
        alphakkprime <- alphak[i] + alphak[j] - 1 + prod(fractval)
        }
    varcontrib[i, j] <- ystark[i] * ystark[j] / alphakkprime *
     (alphakkprime/(alphak[i]*alphak[j]) - 1)
    }}

`·.,,  ><(((º>   `·.,,  ><(((º>   `·.,,  ><(((º>

messages.subject: Re: How to handle colors
messages.body_plain:
In S-PLUS, each device has a fixed set of colors -- the color table --
defined when the device is opened.  Color numbers refer to a color in the
color table.  This applies to all devices (e.g. graphsheet, postscript,
pdf.graph), and each device has its own color table.  The color table
generally cannot be changed after the device has been opened, and in
particular par() has no effect on the color table other than selecting the
currently active color.

The way color tables are defined varies from device to device, but for
example with graphsheet() (i.e. the graph window on the Windows version --
you don't mention which version or device you are using) you can either use
the color.table argument, or re-define one of the color schemes in Options >
Color Schemes and (for example) call graphsheet(color.scheme="user 1") to
upen a graphics window with your selected color scheme.  To view the color
table for an open graphsheet, right-click in the blue area off the page and
choose "Colors..." and click the "User Colors" button.  The color table is
listed in the Custom Colors section, ordered like this:

0  2  4  6  8 10 12 14
1  3  5  7  9 11 13 15

In the default color scheme, green is color 3.

On a tangential note, I'm ashamed to discover that despite just typing the
word color about twenty times, I never had to backspace the letter u.  Sigh.

# David Smith

messages.subject: Summary: Using Numerical Recipies in C with S on S+2000
messages.subject_clean: Summary: Using Numerical Recipies in C with S on S+2000
messages.body_plain:
As I writting C code for S+2000 using routines from Numerical Recipies
in C, I found that 'vector' is defined and used extensively by the 
Numerical Recipies in C (see NRUTIL.H) and by Splus (see S.h). 
Yeng Bun and Bill Dunlap from insightfull offered the following 
comments. Thank you.

Gabriel Baud-Bovy

>From Bill Dunlap:

'vector' is no longer in the Splus include files for Splus6.0.
(Well, it is there but it is surrounded by #ifdef's so it generally
isn't visible except for those with old code.)  We tried to get
rid of a bunch of commonly used definitions, like TRUE and FALSE.

As for Splus 2000, you are best off splitting your code in 2
parts and using different include files for the 2 parts (or
using #ifdef's in one include file).

>From Yeng Bun:

The typedef of vector in S.h is virtually gone from S+6.  It is not
defined unless the macro S_COMPATIBILITY is defined to some value.  S+6
uses s_object in place of vector. Here are the lines from S_struct.h
included in S.h:

#if defined(S_COMPATIBILITY) && S_COMPATIBILITY>=10 && !defined(vector)
typedef struct s_object_struct vector;
#endif

RAM. This works well. I'm doing basic and intermediate things,
nothing special, and I have found only slight syntax differences
between S-Plus and R. I'm using R more often than S-Plus, but I
wouldn't say that one or the other is superior.

In my opinion, R has three advantages:
1) Prize: it's free!
2) It has lower system requirements. It needs fewer system
ressources than S-Plus. You can even have multiple sessions of R
open at the same time!
3) It's faster to use because you don't get distracted by too
many menues, pop-ups and options. Only command language.

And three disadvantages:
1) It's a bit buggy. On my system (Windows NT 4.0) R tends to
crash 1-2 times per day.
2) It seems to be slower than S when you use build-in algorithms
that require lots of computation.
3) Producing good-looking charts with R is a pain!

Hope that helped,
Jens Hanisch

messages.body_plain:
Dear S+users,

Along with some recent questions about memory management, I have
the following question (I use S+2000 on W2000 with 256M RAM). I 
have a relatively large dataset (dim=640891x8,object.size=30MB)on 
which I am doing simple extracting operations:

assign("data",data[data$rt<1000,],w=1,immediate=T)
assign("data",data[data$ext<1000,],w=1,immediate=T)
assign("data",data[data$x1>3000,],w=1,immediate=T)
etc.

when I execute these lines one by one, I don't have any problem
but when I execute several of them together by highlighting 
them together in my script window, I get a message stating that
S-Plus is unable to allocate the necessary memory. I understand
that I can do something like

index<-data$rt<1000 & data$ext<1000 & data$x1>3000
assign("data",data[index,],w=1,immediate=T)

to solve this issue (I also will install soon more memory on
my PC) but I don't understand why it is not working
in the previous manner. I thought that using immediate=T ensured
that the object was not retained in memory for future use
(S programming. p. 58 and 178). What cause this hunger for
memory in S+ if not the backout mechanism? Would S+6.0 do 
better? And if so, why?

As usual, I will post a summary of replies. Thank you.

Gabriel Baud-Bovy

I am estimating the following nested models with SPLUS 2000 in a PC:

Model 1)
coxph(formula = Surv(ANOI, ANOF, CENSURA) ~ log(SIZE) + INTER + PROFI +
PROXIC + PROXIE + DENSI + MGROW + DEPHA + OBJEH + NUMSB + CMOBC + NMARK +
(NMARK^2) + MMKC + cluster(NCAJA), data = datos, na.action = na.omit, eps
= 0.0001, iter.max = 100, method ="efron", robust = T)

Model 2)
coxph(formula = Surv(ANOI, ANOF, CENSURA) ~ log(SIZE) + INTER + PROFI +
PROXIC + PROXIE + DENSI + MGROW + DEPHA + OBJEH + NUMSB + CMOBC + NMARK +
(NMARK^2) + MMKC + I(MMKC^2) + cluster(NCAJA), data = datos, na.action =
na.omit, eps = 0.0001, iter.max = 100, method ="efron", robust = T)

Together with the output, I receive the usual information of the LR, Wald
and Score tests and a note that says:

     observations within a cluster, the Wald and robust score tests do
not)."

Does this message mean I cannot use the LR test for comparison between
these nested models? If so, which is the alternative? How can I test
whether model 2 is better or worse than model 1?

Your help is appreciated.

Jaime Gomez

messages.subject: No random effects in nlme--Summary
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Bill Pikounis, Brian D. Ripley, Douglas Bates, Andrew Robinson, Jack Lewis, Jose' Pinheiro, and Tero Lakkala for taking time to reply.  The answer is 'You cannot estimate a purely fixed effects model in nlme()'.  Instead you use gnls(), which is essentially the fixed-effects version of nlme().

Comment. To use anova()  to compare a random-effects model using nlme() to its fixed-effects-only version using gnls(), you must specify 'method=ML' in nlme().  If you use 'method=REML', anova() then complains you're not comparing models estimated by the same method, a perfectly legitimate complaint.

messages.subject: Query on nls
messages.body_plain:
To whom can help :

I made a program in which I am using the S+ "nls" function to estimate some
parameters of a given formula. Globally :

        estimation <- nls( ... parameters passed to the function...)
        ep <- estimation$parameters
        se <- summary(estimation)
        tsep <- t(se$parameters)
        SE.beta <- tsep[2, 2]   # for local purpose
        T.beta <- tsep[3, 2]    # for local purpose
        results[i,  ] <- c(ep, SE.beta, T.beta) 

Note : "results" is a data frame. Actually, the program runs line by line on
a data frame of given values [using a loop : for (i in 1:N)
{...instructions...}], so that for each line of given values it computes the
parameters of the formula modelizing these values. Then, the ith call of the
program writes the estimated parameters in the ith line of the "results"
file.

Everything works well as far as nls converges.

If nls doesn't converge :

The simple program I made has undesirable consequences : the procedure
stops, the program is dumped, and no information is written to the file of
results.  So that if lines 1 to N are being treated by the program and if
nls doesn't converge for line N, I don't retrieve anything at all : the
results for the preceeding lines, even previously computed, are lost as the
"results" file is void.

The problem I have with nls is that I don't know how to skip such a step.
What I would like to do in a case of non convergence of nls is :

- writing for example in the file of results a line of NA values,
- making the procedure go nevertheless to the next line.

Then, I could pass to the program in one instruction all lines of given
values, and I could get a complete "results" file : either with  estimated
parameters if the estimation process succeeded, or with NAs is estimation
process failed.

Can anyone help me to resolve this problem ?

Thanks and regards,

Andre MERY
Aventis Pharma France
andre.mery at aventis.com

messages.subject: Re: Continuous Time Dependent Covariates in Cox Proportional Hazards Model
messages.subject_clean: Continuous Time Dependent Covariates in Cox Proportional Hazards Model
messages.body_plain:
Matt Soukup asks whether coxph can accomodate a continuous time-dependent
covariate.
  Short answer: No.
  
  Long answer:
    1. The most common use of such variables is to test for proportional
hazards.  For that purpose, the cox.zph function is far superior to adding
a covariate.  (It's for exactly the same reason that a linear fit with a
scatterplot is better than one without a plot --- outliers can have a big
impact and the plot shows them).

    2. In the rare case that you want a continuous variable for it's own
sake (twice in my career for me), you can create a very big data set.  Let
u[i] be the vector of unique event times.  A data set with time intervals of
0 to u[1], u[1] to u[2], ...., i.e., as (start,stop] data set, will give the
same results as a true time-dependent covariate.  

        Terry Therneau

messages.subject: Re: Query on nls
messages.body_plain:
You need to make use of the try() function.  You don't give your version
of `S+', but it's there in all recent versions (but not 3.4 nor 4.5, say).
Unfortunately it has no documentation prior to 6.0 (except in `S
Programming').

Use

estimation <- try(nls( ... parameters passed to the function...))
if(inherits(estimation, "Error")) {
   set returns to NA
} else {
   set normal returns
}

messages.subject: Re: Splus6 and Splus2000
messages.body_plain:
Shilpi:

Careful! 

!is.element(tmp1,dp)||tmp2 <=2   ## note the double ||

gives T and will evaluate as you wanted. The reason is that the logical
evaluation is carried out from left to right only so far as is needed to
determine the result, so the tmp2<2 expression is not even seen once the
truth of the expression to the left of || is determined.

This is obbviously not true of the VECTORIZED evaluation with |. If this is
truly what you want, then you certainly have identified a nasty trap between
S4 and S3.

Cheers,

messages.subject: How to get rid of multiple elements without a loop?
messages.subject_clean: How to get rid of multiple elements without a loop?
messages.body_plain:
I'm not an expert with S-plus and I hope that this one is not too elementary
for you.

I have a large data vector. It has a several same values (strings) in
arbitrary order and I would like to remove those all the multiple instances.
So "b", "a", "b", "c" should become "b", "a", "c" or "a", "b", "c" - order
doesn't matter.

I made a short code for that but as a loop its very slow. Would you have any
suggestion how to make a loopless solution. I have tried For-BATCH which
worked fine from the command line but there seems to be a bug to prevent it
usefulness inside of a function? 

Below is my simple and slow for-function. Thank you in advance.

Jussi Makinen
Risk Analyst
Tapiola Asset Management Ltd.

***

data.vector <- c("b", "a", "b", "c")

"as.one.instance" <- function(data.vector)
{
        len <- length(data.vector)

        valid.data <- vector()

        for(i in 1:(len-1)) {
                if( !is.element(data.vector[i], data.vector[(i+1):len]) )
valid.data[i] <- data.vector[i]
        }
        valid.data[len] <- data.vector[len]
        valid.data <- valid.data[!(valid.data == "NA") &
!is.all.white(valid.data)]
        
valid.data
}

> a <- c("b", "a", "b", "c")
> as.one.instance(a)
[1] "a" "b" "c"

messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Brian Ripley and Jim Pratt who mentioned that memory is
not freed up when several lines are executed in the script window
until successful completion even with the immediate=T option in 
the assign function. 

See my original question annotated by Brian Ripley message for
more details below.

Gabriel Baud-Bovy

>> Dear S+users,
>>
>> Along with some recent questions about memory management, I have
>> the following question (I use S+2000 on W2000 with 256M RAM). I
>> have a relatively large dataset (dim=640891x8,object.size=30MB)on
>> which I am doing simple extracting operations:
>>
>> assign("data",data[data$rt<1000,],w=1,immediate=T)
>> assign("data",data[data$ext<1000,],w=1,immediate=T)
>> assign("data",data[data$x1>3000,],w=1,immediate=T)
>> etc.
>>
>> when I execute these lines one by one, I don't have any problem
>> but when I execute several of them together by highlighting
>> them together in my script window, I get a message stating that
>> S-Plus is unable to allocate the necessary memory. I understand
>> that I can do something like
>>
>> index<-data$rt<1000 & data$ext<1000 & data$x1>3000
>> assign("data",data[index,],w=1,immediate=T)
>>
>> to solve this issue (I also will install soon more memory on
>> my PC) but I don't understand why it is not working
>> in the previous manner. I thought that using immediate=T ensured
>> that the object was not retained in memory for future use
>> (S programming. p. 58 and 178). What cause this hunger for
>> memory in S+ if not the backout mechanism? Would S+6.0 do
>> better? And if so, why?
>
>The problem is that you submitted from a script window.  That is
>like source()-ing a file: if any command fails the whole submission is
>backed-out.  So `immediate=T' seems to have no effect.
>
>Either paste into the commands window, or use a script via sqpe < foo.q.
>The last uses least mempry in my experience.
>
>It is likely that S+6.0 would use less memory, as it is much more
>careful not to make copies of objects in memory.
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

thanks to B. Ripley and N. Ellis for their replies.  Prof. Ripley said that
"the recycling rule differs in S4 from S3 (and hence in 6.0 from 2000).
Empty components give empty results in S4, NAs in S3."  This could explain
the error messages I was getting, he also expressed the opinion that this
behaviour, the current one, is more rational than the old one.  Personnally
I don't have an opinion on the subject, I only observe that backward
compatibility is getting hit.

Nick suggested testing for the offending condition before doing the
assignement, which is what I was trying to avoid and furthermore it is hard
under the new S4 engine to test for such conditions.  When a character
variable has the value "character(0)",

is.na(char.var) will return logical(0),
is.character(char.var) will return True,
is.null(char.var) will return False
nchar(char.var) will return numeric(0)
length(char.var) will return 0,

the last instruction is the only way I found, so far, for checking for that
condition, is there other ways of checking for such conditions?  The same
applies for numeric variables.  The original message follows.

Thanks again to Prof. Ripley and Nick Ellis,

Gérald Jean
Analyste-conseil (statistiques), Actuariat

  len          <- length(Differentiel)

                             'Final.Coef' = coef.final,

  out[intersection,c('Freq.Diff', 'Freq.t')] <- ttt.1[intersection,

ce 6 rows

if one finds how, for "character(0)" would make the already long function

messages.subject: Fitting Pareto dist in a mixture
messages.subject_clean: Fitting Pareto dist in a mixture
messages.body_plain:
Dear all:
First, apologies for cross-posting multiplicities and for a query that is
more
analytically related than S-language related.

The bottom-line wish is:

Could you please provide and advice, references, etc on S software
approaches for
fitting a distribution with density:

p*g(x) + (1-p)*f(x) 

where g(x) is the familiar lognormal 2-parameter density
and f(x) is Pareto as defined below?

Here is the lengthier story:
I am collaborating with a scientific colleague who has constructed a
database
of binding assay data, namely EC/IC50's across a wide variety of chemical
entities and experimental conditions.  Among other things, he has an
interest
in characterizing tails of the distribution.  We have been studying various
fields in the literature to get a sense of what density forms we should
focus
on.

In addition to lognormal, weibull, & gamma, we found several references to
the
Pareto distribution.  It is of course easy enough to fit all of these with
existing S language functions (and reference to MASS and S Programming), and
even when considering lognormal mixtures as we are.

However, I have been attempting to use the Pareto
density form 

f(x) = ( a *  k^a  ) / ( x^{a + 1} ) ; k > 0, a > 0, x >= k

as part of a mixture with a lognormal.  Reparametrizing the density to 

f(x) = ( a *  k^a  ) / ( (x + k)^{a + 1} ) ; k > 0, a > 0, x > 0

seems to help but the optimization routines remain balky and / or give
convergences that do not make sense to me.  (I understand that starting
values, scales, etc. are very important.) I suspect that the support aspect
of
the Pareto ( i.e.  f(x) > 0 only for x >= k ) imposes an indentifiability
problem with the mixing proportion parameter.

Again, any advice is welcome.

Thanks in advance,
Bill

messages.subject: Summary: Continuous Time Dependent Covariates in Cox Proportional Hazards Model
messages.subject_clean: Summary: Continuous Time Dependent Covariates in Cox Proportional Hazards Model
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Jan Brogger and Terry Therneau for their quick replies. Terry
pointed out that often times, continuous time dependent covariates are
used to test for proportional hazards. This is exactly what I was trying
to accomplish and his comments follow. Jan also gave a URL for how one
can create something similar to continuous covariates in Stata, which
gives an type of recipe on how to create the covariate in Splus, this
also follows.

Mat

THE URL:

http://www.stata.com/support/faqs/stat/stcox.html

Terry's comments:

Mat Soukup asks whether coxph can accomodate a continuous time-dependent

covariate. 

Short answer: No. 

Long answer: 

1. The most common use of such variables is to test for proportional

hazards. For that purpose, the cox.zph function is far superior to adding

a covariate. (It's for exactly the same reason that a linear fit with a

scatterplot is better than one without a plot --- outliers can have a big

impact and the plot shows them).

2. In the rare case that you want a continuous variable for it's own

sake (twice in my career for me), you can create a very big data set. Let

u[i] be the vector of unique event times. A data set with time intervals
of 

0 to u[1], u[1] to u[2], ...., i.e., as (start,stop] data set, will give
the 

same results as a true time-dependent covariate. 

Mat Soukup 

University of Virginia 

Department of Statistics 

804.924.3066 (office) 

mjs5b at virginia.edu

messages.subject: summary: negative binomial glms and extractAIC
messages.subject_clean: summary: negative binomial glms and extractAIC
messages.body_plain:
A couple of weeks back I posted a query about extractAIC( ) returning
negative values when used with the MASS library function glm.nb( ) for
fitting glms with negative binomial error distributions. Many thanks to
the illuminating answers from Brian Ripley and Bill Venables.

In summary, the negative AIC values arise from leaving a large negative
constant out of the log likelihood. As per Brian Ripley's suggestion
inserting the missing term makes the AIC's positive. However, as all
model selection inference is relative to the model with the minimum AIC,
the differences between the AIC's for the models are identical whether
the constant is in or not.

Bill Venables asked whether the results made sense. The short answer is
yes, with two caveats. First, for some models the iteration that
estimates theta (the dispersion parameter) shoots off wildly and forces
theta towards zero which produces nonsense. These cases are readily
identifiable afterwards!  Second, some negative coefficients get very
large, with large standard errors - this seems to occur in the same
context described for problems with binomial glms in MASS (pg 225, the
Hauck-Donner phenomenon), where a group of values is all zero and the
glm is trying to set the linear predictor to minus infinity. At the
moment I'm interpreting this to indicate that particular combination of
samples is unlikely to be a result of sampling from a negative binomial
distribution with a positive mean, which, if true, will be a good thing
for my application.

Thanks again!

Cheers,
Drew

--

Dept. of Zoology and Entomology,

.Audit is used to keep a record of all the commands entered.  This could
be examined via

Splus AUDIT

in S-PLUS 3.4, but that seems missing in 5.1.

It's possible to make .Data/.Audit unwriteable, when nothing is
recorded.  As in

chmod u-w .Data/.Audit

This will give a warning you can ignore.

last.dump is the last dump from an error, set because the default for
options(error=dump.calls) dumps the calls in that object.  It's likely to
be small unless options(error=dump.frames) is used.  If you know what you
are doing and really don't want it, set options(error=dump.calls).

(Y_1,..,Y_n) against a particular continuous variable. The values of the
response variable are the estimated coefficients of a factor
(Y_1=Beta_1,..Y_n=Beta_n) obtained with a previous GLM. Given the

I have extracted from the covariance matrix of the first GLM, the
covariance between the Beta_i and I try to find (without success!) a way
to introduce this matrix in the correlation structure of the gls
function.
Can anybody help me?

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Under Windows NT on Splus 4.5, I try to read a text file which contains in column 1 dates and in column 2 numbers. Here are the first few lines of the file:

12-Dec-85                                         10.05

04-Jan-86                                         10.55

11-Feb-86                                         10.26

13-Mar-86                                          9.79

15-Apr-86                                          9.83

First, I read the data in vec:

> vec <- scan(file = "D:\\timeseries.txt", what = list("character", numeric()))

After, I construct an univariate time series with arbitrary sampling time intervals in ts0:

> ts0 _ its(vec[[2]],times=dates(vec[[1]], format = "day-mon-yr"))

Error in its(vec[[2]], times = dates(vec[[1]], format = "day-mon-y..: times not in ascending order

Dumped

As you see, the error message seems to indicate that dates in my file are not in ascending order. I found after many tries that the problem concerns year 2000 dates. The command

        

> ts0 _ its(vec[[2]][1:2334],times=dates(vec[[1]][1:2334], format = "day-mon-yr"))

returns no error message and

        

> ts0 _ its(vec[[2]][1:2335],times=dates(vec[[1]][1:2335], format = "day-mon-yr"))

returns the same error message as above. Here is the vector of dates around 2335:

> vec[[1]][2333:2336]

[1] "30-Dec-99" "31-Dec-99" "04-Jan-00" "05-Jan-00"

> dates(vec[[1]][2333:2336],format="day-mon-year")

[1] 12/30/99 12/31/99 01/04/0  01/05/0 

The 2335th element is the first occurence in my file of year 2000. Now, if you sort the vector, the result is:

> sort(dates(vec[[1]][2333:2336],format="day-mon-yr"))

[1] 01/04/0  01/05/0  12/30/99 12/31/99

S-Plus seems to consider 01/04/0 as 01/04/1900 (which obviously is less than 12/30/1999). Is there a setting that you can set to tell S-Plus to consider 99 as 1999 and 00 as 2000?

Thank you very much,

Patrick

messages.subject: .Fortran call of DLL causing Splus exit
messages.subject_clean: .Fortran call of DLL causing Splus exit
messages.body_plain:
Dear S-Plus users,

I am having trouble using a fortran-compiled DLL in Splus.
Briefly, a function call to the fortran-compiled DLL causes an exit from S-PLUS!
After reading several posts related to linking fortan to Splus via DLLs'
(posted on the S-user archives), I am still having problems.
I have spent several days trying to narrow in on the problem. I am nearing my
wits end.

Platform Details: I'm working on Windows 95, using Splus-2000 (Release 1) and
using Fortran Powerstation 4.0.

My most direct question is how can i get Splus to give me some clues about the
type
of error that is causing it to exit.  I describe the specifics of my problem in
more detail below.

I have the following code in my Fortran program which as I understand acts as a
substitute for a formal .DEF file.

                    !MS$ATTRIBUTES DLLEXPORT :: MYFUN

(it occurs as one of the first statements in my main fortran subroutine)

I up-load the DLL file in Splus using the following code

     if(!is.dll.loaded("myfun.dll")) {
          dll.load("C:\\MSDEV\\Projects\\myfun\\Debug\\myfun.dll", symbols =
list(myfun =
               "_MYFUN@56"))
     }

I have used Windows-explorer (Quick-view) to examine my DLL, confirming that it
does indeed declare a symbol for my fortran Subroutine.  That symbol's
definition,
     _MYFUN@56

is compatible with the command I've used in the call to dll.load.
(BTW, I'm told the 56 makes sense.  I understand from previous posts that it
represents
the number of arguments times 4 ... I have 14 arguments to myfun)

Finally, I have an splus calling function which calls the Fortran symbol.  The
relevant
code is as follows.

     storage.mode(x1) <- "integer"
     storage.mode(x2) <- "integer"
     storage.mode(x3) <- "single"
     :    :    :    :
     storage.mode(x14) <- "single"
     res <- .Fortran("myfun",
          x1,
          x2,
          x3 = X3,
          ::    ::,
          x14)

The argument order and type are consistent between the Splus and Fortran code.
Note also that exact same code worked on a unix platform
(albeit with dyn.load replacing the role of dll.load), which seems to confirm
to me that the arguments must be compatable!

When I run my Splus program, the dll loads successfully
however the first call the the fortran subroutine causes an exit from Splus
(leaving me
no explicit clues regarding the problem).

I think I can ruel out the following.
1. A simple mismatch in argument type or order.
     - A dummy version of my DLL consisting of only the subroutine definition
     including all arguments and a few rudimentary expressions works succesfully
     (i.e., as a. Fortran call in splus).
     - The exact same code worked on Unix platform using dyn.load()
2. An obvious problem with the fortran code
     - I have set-up a main program in fortran and called the very same Fortran
subroutine
     constituting the DLL.  It works.  This suggests to me that the problem lies
 in the
     interface between Splus and the compiler.

 I have tried all the sensible permutations for call.convention and MS
attributes in
the fortran code.  None of them work.

I would be greatly appreciative of any suggestions about what to
be on the look out for.  Are Unix compilers known to be more forgiving about
certain details than Windows compilers ?

Some added detail is shown below for those who are interested.

My suspicions
1. My fortran program calls several other subroutines (but they were compiled as
 part
of the DLL making process).  Could this be causing problems?

2. I pass several arrays from Splus to the fortran subroutine and then from
there
to several other subroutines.  My approach here has been to pass the dimensions
along as separate arguments in the subroutines, and dimension accordingly.
Perhaps
the Splus interface imposes tougher restrictions?

3. Perhaps I require an explicit DEF file rather than the DLLEXPORT option (does

anyone have an example DEF file for me to draw from).  This may allow me to be
explicit about which arguments require pointer-references rather than
value-references
(i.e., the arrays).

messages.body_plain:
Sincere thanks to Nick Ellis for his blisteringly fast response to my 
query.  His "reshape" function (pasted below) does exactly what I want.

Todd Hatfield

reshape(air,,1:4)
where
reshape <-
function(obj, col.copy = NULL, col.unfold = 1:dim(obj)[2], label = "label",
value = "value")
{
n <- dim(obj)[1]
p <- length(col.unfold)
res <- vector("list", length(col.copy) + 2)
names(res) <- c(if(is.null(col.copy)) NULL else dimnames(obj[,
col.copy, drop = F])[[2]], label, value)
for(i in seq(along = col.copy)) {
res[[i]] <- rep(obj[, col.copy[i]], p)
}
res[[label]] <- rep(dimnames(obj[, col.unfold, drop = F])[[2]],
rep(n, p))
res[[value]] <- as.vector(data.matrix(obj[, col.unfold, drop = F]))
as.data.frame(res)
}

messages.subject: summary - detecting spatial units that have no neighbors
messages.subject_clean: summary - detecting spatial units that have no neighbors
messages.body_plain:
A belated thanks to Stephen Kaluzny and Nick Ellis for
pointing out that the check.islands function in S+Spatial
Stats will not do what I was trying to do. A special thanks
to Nick Ellis for providing me a function that is able
detect  spatial units that have no neighbors. Their reply's
are given below but first here is the original posting:

> My problem is that I would like to detect spatial units
that
> have no neighbors using the
> "check.islands" function that comes with  the
> S+SpatialStats module. For  example  a matrix
>   x <- matrix(1,ncol=5,nrow=4)
>   x[3,] <- x[,4] <- 0
>   x
>      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [,5]
> [1,]    1    1    1    0    1
> [2,]    1    1    1    0    1
> [3,]    0    0    0    0    0
> [4,]    1    1    1    0    1
> has four "islands" (1-land , 0-water). In general, how can

> one calculate the number of islands
> for any configuration stored in a matrix  using the
> S+SpatialStats module?

Stephen wrote:

The check.islands function requires a spatial.neighbor
object. If you
have a matrix of neighbor weights then you can construct a
spatial.neighbor object using the function spatial.neighbor.
A matrix of
neighbor weights must be a square matrix such that if
element [i,j] is
non-zero, then spatial regions j is considered a neighbor of
region i.
The neighbor relation is not considered symmetric by
default; [i,j] in
the neighbor weights matrix being non-zero means that j is a
neighbor of
i but unless [j,i] is non-zero in the neighbor weights
matrix, i is not a
neighbor of j.

The check.islands function shows those regions that have no
neighbors
AND are not neighbors of any other region.  (The summary
method for
objects of class spatial.neighbor also shows this
information).

Your matrix is not square so I do not know what the value
represent.
If your x was:

        > x <- matrix(1,ncol=5,nrow=5)  # a square matrix
        > x[3,] <- x[,4] <- 0

        > x
             [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [,5]
        [1,]    1    1    1    0    1
        [2,]    1    1    1    0    1
        [3,]    0    0    0    0    0
        [4,]    1    1    1    0    1
        [5,]    1    1    1    0    1

Then you can create a spatial.neighbor object:

        > snx <- spatial.neighbor(neighbor.matrix=x)

But this does not have any islands:

        > summary(snx)
        Matrix was NOT defined as symmetric
        Number of Regions: 5
        Average Number of Connections: 4
        Average Weight: 1
        Least Number of Connections: 4 for Regions with
Indices:
        [1] 1 2 4 5
        Maximum Number of Connections: 4 for Regions with
Indices:
        [1] 1 2 4 5
        Missing Row Indices:
        [1] 3
        Missing Column Indices:
        [1] 4
        Indices of Regions with No Connections (islands):
        [1] "none"

This shows that location 3 has no neighbors yet it is the
neighbor for
some locations and location 4 is not the neighbor for any
location
but it has neighbors.

Hope this explanation helps.

Stephen Kaluzny (spk at insightful.com)
Insightful Corp.
---------------------------------------------------

and Nick Ellis wrote:

An 'island' in the sense of the check.islands function is a
single point
without neighbours, so that, by that definition your example
would have only
1 island.

Below is a way of finding the islands (let's call them
continents) in your
example.
[....]

==========================================================================

x <- matrix(1,ncol=5,nrow=4)
x[3,] <- x[,4] <- 0 # matrix with 4 'continents'
x
xpad <- matrix(0,6,7) # padded version (for indexing below)
xpad[2:5,2:6] <- x
i <- matrix(1:20,4,5) # index for each of the 4x5 points
ipad <- matrix(0,6,7) # padded version
ipad[2:5,2:6] <- i
ipad
right<-ncol(xpad);left<-1;top<-1;bottom<-nrow(xpad)

# find all neighbours: a neighbour is point to immediate N S
E W NE SE SW or
NW
nhbr <- rbind(
cbind(ipad[,-right][(xpad[,-right]==1)
&(xpad[,-right]==xpad[,-left])],ipad[,-left][(xpad[,-left]==1)

&(xpad[,-right]==xpad[,-left])]),
cbind(ipad[-bottom,][(xpad[-bottom,]==1)
&(xpad[-bottom,]==xpad[-top,])],ipad[-top,][(xpad[-top,]==1)

&(xpad[-bottom,]==xpad[-top,])]),
cbind(ipad[-bottom,-right][(xpad[-bottom,-right]==1)
&(xpad[-bottom,-right]==xpad[-top,-left])],ipad[-top,-left][(xpad[-top,-left

]==1) &(xpad[-bottom,-right]==xpad[-top,-left])]),
cbind(ipad[-bottom,-left][(xpad[-bottom,-left]==1)
&(xpad[-bottom,-left]==xpad[-top,-right])],ipad[-top,-right][(xpad[-top,-rig

ht]==1) &(xpad[-bottom,-left]==xpad[-top,-right])]),
)
nhbr <- rbind(nhbr,nhbr[,2:1]) # if a neighbours b then b
neighbours a
nhbr <- nhbr[order(nhbr[,1]),]
nhbr
xbig <- matrix(0,20,20) # 20 x 20 neighbourhood matrix for
the 20 points in
the 4x5 matrix x
xbig[nhbr] <- 1
diag(xbig) <- 1 # a neighbours a
# Note this means the following 'sea' points are neighbours
of themselves
3,7,11,13:16,19
xprod <- xbig # xprod will find all points in same
'continent'
prev <- xprod*0
while (any(prev!=xprod)) {
        prev <- xprod
        xprod <- (xprod%*%xbig > 0)+0
}
xprod <-
xprod[!duplicated(apply(xprod,1,paste,collapse=".")    ),] #
xprod
has unique rows showing constituents of each continent
lapply(1:nrow(xprod),function(i) (1:20)[xprod[i,]>0]) # a
list of the
'continents' (contiguous land masses, includes 'sea')
sea <- c(3,7,11,13:16,19)
lst <- lapply(1:nrow(xprod),function(i)
(1:20)[-sea][xprod[i,-sea]>0])
lst[sapply(lst,length)>0] # a list of the 'continents'
(contiguous land
masses, excludes 'sea')

# The number of contintents is the length(lst)
==========================================================================

Australia                       http://www.marine.csiro.au

Again, many thanks Nick.

Cheers,
Mrigesh

messages.subject: Re: .Fortran call of DLL causing Splus exit
messages.subject_clean: .Fortran call of DLL causing Splus exit
messages.body_plain:
I sent a reply yesterday but I am not sure if it went through. However,
today I am running into a similar problem. When you get a stack overflow
in the dll Splus simply exits. This happens because you may be creating
a temporary large data structure in the Fortran and Splus allows very
limited stack space for the dll. The way to solve it is to pass the
large data structures from Splus to the fortran in the fortran call. For
example
suppose you use Work(dimrow,dimcol) in your dll.

Create this matrix in Splus (eg  Workmat<-rep(0,dimrow*dimcol))

add it to your Fortran call.
.Fortran(v1,v2,....Workmat)

This allows Splus to allocate the memory for the variable instead of
the Fortran DLL.  I suspect things (or limits) work differently in Unix
and the dummy function you tested probably uses a smaller data set.

Hope this helps,

Michael Conklin

Briefly, a function call to the fortran-compiled DLL causes an exit
from S-PLUS!
After reading several posts related to linking fortan to Splus via
DLLs'
(posted on the S-user archives), I am still having problems.
I have spent several days trying to narrow in on the problem. I am
nearing my
wits end.

Platform Details: I'm working on Windows 95, using Splus-2000 (Release
1) and
using Fortran Powerstation 4.0.

My most direct question is how can i get Splus to give me some clues
about the
type
of error that is causing it to exit.  I describe the specifics of my
problem in
more detail below.

I have the following code in my Fortran program which as I understand
acts as a
substitute for a formal .DEF file.

                    !MS$ATTRIBUTES DLLEXPORT :: MYFUN

(it occurs as one of the first statements in my main fortran
subroutine)

I up-load the DLL file in Splus using the following code

     if(!is.dll.loaded("myfun.dll")) {
          dll.load("C:\\MSDEV\\Projects\\myfun\\Debug\\myfun.dll",
symbols =
list(myfun =
               "_MYFUN@56"))
     }

I have used Windows-explorer (Quick-view) to examine my DLL, confirming
that it
does indeed declare a symbol for my fortran Subroutine.  That symbol's
definition,
     _MYFUN@56

is compatible with the command I've used in the call to dll.load.
(BTW, I'm told the 56 makes sense.  I understand from previous posts
that it
represents
the number of arguments times 4 ... I have 14 arguments to myfun)

Finally, I have an splus calling function which calls the Fortran
symbol.  The
relevant
code is as follows.

     storage.mode(x1) <- "integer"
     storage.mode(x2) <- "integer"
     storage.mode(x3) <- "single"
     :    :    :    :
     storage.mode(x14) <- "single"
     res <- .Fortran("myfun",
          x1,
          x2,
          x3 = X3,
          ::    ::,
          x14)

The argument order and type are consistent between the Splus and
Fortran code.
Note also that exact same code worked on a unix platform
(albeit with dyn.load replacing the role of dll.load), which seems to
confirm
to me that the arguments must be compatable!

When I run my Splus program, the dll loads successfully
however the first call the the fortran subroutine causes an exit from
Splus
(leaving me
no explicit clues regarding the problem).

I think I can ruel out the following.
1. A simple mismatch in argument type or order.
     - A dummy version of my DLL consisting of only the subroutine
definition
     including all arguments and a few rudimentary expressions works
succesfully
     (i.e., as a. Fortran call in splus).
     - The exact same code worked on Unix platform using dyn.load()
2. An obvious problem with the fortran code
     - I have set-up a main program in fortran and called the very same
Fortran
subroutine
     constituting the DLL.  It works.  This suggests to me that the
problem lies
 in the
     interface between Splus and the compiler.

 I have tried all the sensible permutations for call.convention and MS
attributes in
the fortran code.  None of them work.

I would be greatly appreciative of any suggestions about what to
be on the look out for.  Are Unix compilers known to be more forgiving
about
certain details than Windows compilers ?

Some added detail is shown below for those who are interested.

My suspicions
1. My fortran program calls several other subroutines (but they were
compiled as
 part
of the DLL making process).  Could this be causing problems?

2. I pass several arrays from Splus to the fortran subroutine and then
from
there
to several other subroutines.  My approach here has been to pass the
dimensions
along as separate arguments in the subroutines, and dimension
accordingly.
Perhaps
the Splus interface imposes tougher restrictions?

3. Perhaps I require an explicit DEF file rather than the DLLEXPORT
option (does

anyone have an example DEF file for me to draw from).  This may allow
me to be
explicit about which arguments require pointer-references rather than
value-references
(i.e., the arrays).
